section1_theta.title: What Varsity teaches about Theta (time decay)
points: All options lose value as expiration approaches; theta is the rate of that value loss per day, all else held equal.
Premium = Intrinsic Value + Time Value; all else equal, an option loses some value every day purely because of theta.

Time decay is non-linear: early in a series (many days left) an option barely loses value day to day; as expiry nears, decay accelerates sharply. Varsity's own illustration: at 120 days to expiry a premium was around 350, but by 100 days to expiry (just 20 days later) it had only fallen to around 300 — a small move for a large chunk of calendar time.
A short (seller) position benefits from theta — the seller's objective is to hold and pocket premium while it erodes in their favour daily.

Consequence: writing early in a series pockets large time-value premium but erosion is slow; writing close to expiry starts from a smaller premium but erodes fast. Mirror image for a buyer (this person's actual side): a fresh monthly (many days left) is a structurally gentler entry than the last week of the same contract, independent of direction.
Indian index options are European-style: a buyer cannot exercise early, only square off before expiry or let it settle at expiry (confirmed directly by Varsity's author in the page's comment thread).

section1_5_vega_iv_crush.title: What Varsity teaches about Vega and IV crush — the THIRD source of premium loss
section1_5_vega_iv_crush.note: This is the piece most retail traders conflate with theta, and it directly matters for a 700–900 premium contract.
points: Vega measures how much an option's premium moves per 1-point change in implied volatility (IV) — independent of whether the underlying spot moves at all.

Delta/Gamma affect the INTRINSIC portion of a premium (driven by spot movement); Theta/Vega affect the EXTRINSIC/time portion — this split was directly confirmed by Varsity's own author in the Vega chapter's comment thread.

Around known events (RBI policy, Union Budget, elections, company earnings), IV typically rises beforehand pricing in uncertainty, then collapses sharply afterward once the event resolves — commonly called 'IV crush.' A premium can fall sharply on IV crush alone, even with zero net theta decay and even if the underlying moved in the buyer's predicted direction, because the vega-driven loss can outweigh the delta-driven gain.

Practical implication for a 700–900 ITM premium: a drop over a few days could be theta (expected), vega/IV crush (event-driven, sudden), intrinsic loss (spot moved against the position), or a mix of all three — and without decomposing the change, these three look identical on a raw price chart.

section2_moneyness.title: What Varsity teaches about Moneyness (ITM/ATM/OTM) and Intrinsic Value
points: Intrinsic value is the amount an option buyer would make if they exercised the contract right now; it can never be negative.
CE intrinsic value = Spot Price − Strike Price. PE intrinsic value = Strike Price − Spot Price.
An option carrying intrinsic value is ITM (In the Money); one with none is OTM (Out of the Money); a strike close to spot is ATM (At the Money).
For calls: every strike below ATM is ITM, every strike above is OTM. For puts: reversed — strikes above ATM are ITM, strikes below are OTM.
Very large intrinsic value = Deep ITM; minimal intrinsic value (opposite side) = Deep OTM.
ITM premiums are always higher than OTM premiums for the same underlying/expiry, since ITM carries intrinsic value on top of remaining time value.
For a buyer's terminal outcome: Varsity's author directly corrected a reader — an option should expire ITM for the buyer to have actually gained anything (not ATM or OTM).

section4_refined_recommendation.title: Refined recommendation (adds precision to the earlier examination report, changes nothing else)
section4_refined_recommendation.why_this_matters: This is a direct, citable, textbook-grounded formula, not a guess — the single highest-value, lowest-risk addition from both the earlier examination and this research pass. It's the one piece of missing math that would have prevented the exact confusion this conversation started from: a large ₹ premium (700–900) looking identical on the dashboard whether it's mostly intrinsic (ITM, low decay risk) or mostly time value (ATM, full decay exposure).

extended_three_way_decomposition.implementation_note: All three inputs (intrinsic formula, existing theta, existing vega × ΔIV) are already available or trivially addable — this decomposition doesn't require any new data source, only combining pieces that already exist separately in the codebase.

section5_what_this_does_not_change: Does not alter the earlier report's finding that a real holiday list (Step 1) is the blocking prerequisite for trading-day-aware calculations.

Does not introduce any new 'engine' — Varsity's own framing (Theta, Moneyness, Intrinsic/Time value) maps cleanly onto Feature Extraction-level calculations, consistent with the earlier architecture recommendation.

Does not change the AI boundary — none of this is Haiku's job to compute; it would only ever explain an already-computed intrinsic/extrinsic/vega split, same as every other deterministic signal in this system.
